newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea strike call over labour law crumbles.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea strike call over labour law crumbles.

text.p: White-collar workers waving balloons joined 40,000 car and shipyard workers in protests on Tuesday, but there were few indications the strike had lived up to its billing as the biggest in South Korea's history.
In the southeast city of Ulsan, about 40,000 workers mostly from the giant Hyundai group's car plants and shipyards held a noisy rally chanting "down with President Kim Young-sam".
Workers wearing red headbands and carrying banners called for a controversial labour law to be repealed as they marched through the city, a traditional hotbed of industrial unrest.
Subways, buses and banks were working normally in Seoul, and for the nation's two biggest ports it was business as usual.
The only disruption in the capital was a lack of taxis.
Scores of workers skirmished with riot police near a Seoul cathedral, where union leaders have sought sanctuary from arrest for organising wildcat stoppages in protest against the law.
The new labour law, pushed through during a clandestine session of parliament on December 26, allows firms to dismiss workers and replace strikers.

Several thousand workers from banks and brokerages waved balloons and sang songs at a "necktie" rally at lunchtime in Seoul's Pagoda Park. Many were dressed in black neckties "to wish death on the labour law", one broker said.
The officially sanctioned Federation of Korean Trade Unions claimed 420,000 of its 1.2 million members were on strike, but the Ministry of Labour said the figure was just over 50,000.
Political analysts said the poor strike response showed the federation had lost its teeth.

Nevertheless, the federation and the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions threatened to continue protests until presidential polls in December and said they would combine forces to defeat the ruling party's candidate.
In their first formal meeting, federation chief Park In-sang and Kwon Young-kil of the more militant confederation said they would carry out the threat if the law was not abolished.

The confederation vowed its 500,000 members would go ahead with indefinite strikes on Wednesday unless the law was scrapped by midnight on Tuesday. Union leaders said the impact of strikes would be more serious if telecommunications workers and subway drivers from the confederation walk out.
"We will concentrate our entire capacity to enforce the full-out strikes," Kwon told a news conference.

The government threatened to take unspecified legal action against international labour leaders who have descended on Seoul in a show of solidarity for strikers. It said they were intervening in the dispute, local media reported.

John Evans, general secretary of the Trade Union Advisory Committee to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), said the activities of the overseas labour leaders were not unusual.
"This is completely normal. The abnormality is the attitude of the government," he told Reuters.
Stock investors took heart from the weak strike response.
The composite index closed at 686.59 points, up 4.1 percent or 27.05 points on the day. Advancing stocks overwhelmed losers 769 to 81, with 60 stocks remaining unchanged.
The government argues a more flexible labour market is urgently needed to help companies cut costs and boost their competitiveness while exports are slumping.
Kim Jung-youl, a fellow at Korea University's Labour Education and Research Institute, said the response by federation members highlighted the group's moderate nature.
"All militant unions, which used to belong to the federation, quit it to form the confederation. A lot of those remaining in the federation are not used to staging strikes," Kim said.
